body_markdown:
A 3-2-1 countdown sends two classic Porsche 911 Turbos racing from a roll down Utah Motorsports Park’s front straight, the unmistakable roar of air-cooled flat-sixes reverberating in their wake.


[Supercar Ron](https://youtu.be/nF5RekIuAYk?t=519) , who initiated the match for his YouTube channel, is driving a gray $1.8 million, 500-hp+ Porsche 911 that Singer “reimagined” as a “Classic Turbo.” His rival in the Guards Red 1986 911 Turbo is 86-year-old Marty Quadland, a retired oral and maxillofacial surgeon, former SCCA racer, and certifiable car nut from age two. Though looking just as it did the day Marty took delivery 40 years ago, the Porsche packs 63 percent more power than stock. Marty seems to get the holeshot, but the video gives victory to the Singer. The closeness of the finish surprised the other 911 owners participating in the track session.


Marty’s modified 930 got the holeshot against a $1.8 million Singer Reimagined Classic Turbo, though the Singer ultimately won.


YouTube/Supercar Ron


The track shindig was near Marty’s summer home, but he’s more likely to be found driving in multi-day sports car tours with his wife, Paula Szypko, than on a drag strip.


“Last fall, we took the Turbo on a four-day trip through Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho,” he says. “This year, we’ve done a couple more of those trips with a different car.”


Marty’s red 1986 Turbo on a Warehouse Club mountain tour.


Courtesy Marty Quadland


He’s got some fun cars to choose from, too. A 1972 de Tomaso Pantera he’s owned since that year recently emerged from a wicked restomod transformation, including a 500-hp Ford 5.2-liter Aluminator replacing the car’s 351 Cleveland. He’s also got a 2015 Lamborghini Huracán and a 2024 Boxster GTS that’s “all hopped up.” A 1936 Ford cabriolet is a sentimental connection to a car he drove in college.


While living in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Marty’s first Western home after retiring, the couple drove the Turbo on tours with the Yellowstone Porsche Club. “I usually did the itineraries, because I’d spent 30-some years riding motorcycles all over the Northwest, and I knew the really fun roads.”


Marty used his 911 Turbo as a daily driver in North Carolina for 20 years, even in occasional snowfalls.


Courtesy Marty Quadland


Decades before enjoying such captivating drives in high-end sports cars, Marty drove his red Turbo as a daily for 20 years in North Carolina, in all weather. The odometer stopped working at 88,706 miles, not long after Marty had the engine souped up in 2010. He estimates the Porsche has at least 120,000 now.


“My athletic endeavors, of which I had many years ago, have really shrunk down to very little, so the cars have been increasingly important for me.”


The odometer on Marty’s Turbo stopped at 88,706 miles. He estimates the car has about 120,000. The 356 seen is an Intermeccanica replica.


Courtesy Marty Quadland


## Starting a Hotrodding Life for $15


Marty was born to drive. At two years old, he’d sit in the driver’s seat of his dad’s 1935 Ford convertible making engine noises. When Marty turned 12, his father bought him a well-worn ’39 Chevy for $15. After playing around with that for a couple of years, Marty sold it for $20 and then built some Ford hot rods, including a chopped ’31 and a ’54 ragtop.


At the end of his freshman year at Dartmouth College in 1959, he bought a green 1936 Ford convertible from a graduating senior for $300, his dad putting up the money. Within weeks, and with two buddies helping, Marty had swapped out the flathead for a souped-up junkyard Chevy 283.


“It could keep up with a Corvette,” he says.


At school, Marty would join other students for some unsanctioned racing on a not-yet-connected stretch of highway under construction. During one such contest at 1:30 in the morning, the Ford’s right rear wheel sheared off, sending the car barreling across a farmer’s front yard and tearing the stairs and the banister off his porch. A worried young Marty apologized profusely to the owner, who said there’d be no problem if he paid for the repairs.


“I had to go to my dad for money again, and that was the last straw. He made me sell the car.”


Next came a Triumph TR3 that Marty drove in some hill climbs. After college, he had only enough money for a very used VW Beetle to drive through dental school at Tufts University in Boston. In 1966, with his first wife pregnant, Marty had to substitute a Fairlane wagon for the Mustang convertible he’d ordered. Completion of school meant answering the draft and serving two years in the Army at Fort Carson in Colorado Springs.


## The Flying Oral Surgeon


The 911 Turbo keeping company with a wicked Pantera restomod in Marty’s Utah car cave.


Courtesy Marty Quadland


After the Army, Marty was off to a three-year residency at The New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center in Manhattan. Finally, working in a practice in North Carolina in 1971, Marty could indulge his car lust. He started with a slightly used 1971 Corvette but soon sold that to get the ’72 Pantera from an owner who had it for just a few months.


The racing bug eventually bit, and Marty spent 25 years competing in the SCCA with a variety of cars: Formula Vee, Formula Ford, Renault spec racer, a GT1 Corvette, and a Radical SR3. In his first race with the Vette, he came from last on the grid to win. For some years, Marty traded part-time racing-school instruction for track time, and he also owned 50 percent of a North Carolina shop that built 356 Speedster and MG-TD replicas.


On the drive home from watching the 1985 24 Hours of Daytona, Marty dropped by Brumos Porsche in Jacksonville and left owning a black 911 Targa. He loved the car and drove it 10,000 miles in a year but then sold it to a fellow doctor. Marty phoned the Brumos sales manager to get a replacement.


“I asked if he had anything I’d be interested in, and he said, ‘How about a Guards Red 911 Turbo?’ I said, ‘I’ll take it.’”


The Turbo stickered at $54,848, including the optional sunroof. Accompanied by his 13-year-old son, Marty flew to Florida and drove the Turbo home.


The first 911 Turbo emerged at a time when Porsche’s option lists were very short.


Courtesy Marty Quadland


## Factory Basics: Porsche 911 Turbo


All current Porsches except the 911 GT3 models and the top-trim Boxsters and Caymans are turbocharged, yet only the most powerful versions in each line wear a “Turbo” badge. That includes, inexplicably, the EVs. Confused? Let’s set the Wayback Machine to a simpler time, when “Porsche Turbo” meant just one thing: 911 Turbo.


Four months after a 911 Carrera RSR Turbo factory racer took second overall at the 1974 24 Hours of Le Mans, Porsche unveiled the 911 Turbo production car at the Paris Auto Show. Cars reached European customers first and came Stateside in late 1975 for the 1976 model year. Porsche marketed the pressurized 911 here as the “Turbo Carrera,” and Porschephiles came to call it by its internal model code, 930.


Porsche marketed the first 911 Turbo as the “Turbo Carrera.”


Porsche


The ’76 Turbo’s staggering $26,000 price was nearly double that of the 165-hp 911S. Its specs seem quaint today. The 3.0-liter flat six used an absurdly low 6.5:1 compression ratio to ward off detonation. A wastegate that held boost to 11.5 PSI was another defense. While the Euro-spec Turbo boasted 260 hp, the U.S. model, using thermal reactors to control emissions, gave 234 hp and 246 lb-ft. of torque. The Turbo’s four-speed manual transmission was geared to take advantage of the torque, though it frustrated drivers. First gear was long enough for 51 mph, and both third and fourth were overdrives, the latter a super-tall 0.65:1.


The first Turbo delivered astounding performance at a time when Corvettes and Ferrari 308s could barely muster 8-second 0-60 sprints. *Car and Driver* got 0-60 in 4.9 seconds and the quarter-mile in 13.5 at 103 mph. Top speed in the test was 156 mph.


Said *Road & Track* : “It takes the driver a moment or two to realize some awesome, unseen force is pushing him back into his seat and thrusting the Carrera forward at an incredible rate.”


That “unseen force” could trigger sudden disaster for drivers caught unaware of the 911’s handling quirks, namely snap-oversteer that earned the early Turbo the ominous “widowmaker” nickname. The 911 Turbo even looked menacing. Widened rear quarters covered wide tires that, along with the unique “whale tail” rear wing, were intended to aid high-speed stability.


A boost in displacement to 3.3 liters and the addition of an intercooler pushed output to 265 hp in the 1978 U.S. 911 Turbo, and Porsche also improved the brakes. Then, unable to meet U.S. emissions standards, Porsche withdrew the Turbo from this market. The big dog returned for 1986 with catalytic converters, Bosch Motronic engine management, and output hiked to 282 hp and 288 lb-ft of torque. The price was also hiked, now double what it was 10 years earlier. Power, acceleration curves, and pricing would rocket skyward over the 911 Turbo’s continued evolution.


## From 282-HP Daily Driver to 461-HP Road Ripper


Marty was still living in North Carolina when he transitioned the Turbo from daily driving to a fun weekend car. For even more fun, he took the car to SpeedWërks, a Porsche performance and racing specialist, for some added pep. The mechanical makeover, completed in fall 2010, included a full top-end rebuild with custom-grind cams. A Garrett GT35 turbo, Kokeln intercooler, and B&B exhaust replaced the factory parts.


This is how you get 461 hp from a first-gen 911 Turbo.


Courtesy Marty Quadland


On the dyno, Marty’s pumped-up Turbo recorded 461 hp and 415 lb-ft. of peak torque. Upgraded anti-roll bars and Bilstein shock inserts tightened handling. To help mitigate the effects of the Porsche’s significant turbo lag, SpeedWërks swapped an even taller first gear and a shorter fourth into the four-speed.


The 3.3-liter engine gives 461 hp and 415 lb-ft of torque, up from the stock 282 and 288 ratings.


Courtesy Marty Quadland


“There’s a little less time for it to unspool during shifts,” Marty says. “Back in the day I would take it up to 155-160, but after the transmission work, top speed dropped 10 or 12 mph. It has no modern tech on it that will save you if you’re stupid, so I take great care of making sure it goes straight.”


## Rocky Mountain High


Marty’s Turbo is usually a reliable partner on long tours, but on the night before the[Hagerty Silver Summit](https://classiccaradventures.com/event/hagerty-silver-summit/) 700-mile excursion around Colorado this past spring, the mighty Porsche died on the road 80 miles from Denver. Just days before, a marque specialist in Salt Lake City had given the Porsche a clean bill of health, but anything can happen to a 40-year-old car.


Marty and wife Paula Szypko on the 2026 Hagerty Silver Summit tour in Colorado.


Meshed House Creative


On the Turbo’s late-afternoon flatbed ride into Denver, Marty and Paula rode in the cab with the driver and his two friendly and sleepy pooches. Marty worked his phone to find area shops that handled air-cooled Porsches, but the first few he reached were booked solid or closing for the day. His last hope, Storz Garage, was closing soon, too, but owner Bob Brown said he’d wait.


Set in a frayed-around-the-edges neighborhood just off Colfax Ave. (Rt. 70), Denver’s main East-West thoroughfare, Storz looked like a closed-up shopfront, with two liquor stores and a tattoo parlor for neighbors. Inside, two big, black dogs stood guard, and the sights and smells reminded Marty of garages from his hotrodding youth. Seeing air-cooled 911s on the lifts was comforting, though.


An electrical gremlin temporarily sidelined the Porsche on the way to the Hagerty Silver Summit.


Paula Szypko


Bob said he’d check the car in the morning, and with the local Enterprise Car Rental closed, he offered the couple his pickup truck and even filled the tank. Marty and Paula joined the other Silver Summit entrants for dinner in Parker that night, hoping for a good outcome.


Bob called in the morning with good news: the Porsche was fixed. He had stayed late to diagnose the problem with help from an electrical expert friend. The engine builder, he explained, had correctly rolled back the two spare wires in the aftermarket ignition box but neglected to insulate them. After 16 years, they’d unrolled and caused a short.


Marty’s big shock came when he heard Bob’s fee: “No charge.”


Seeing Marty gobsmacked by the kind gesture, Bob told him he could send $50 when he got home if that made him feel better. Marty gave it to him on the spot.


Marty took comfort seeing other 911s on the lifts at Storz.


Paula Szypko


“We had a great tour and then drove home with no issues. The whole trip was about 1800 miles.”


Marty wrote Bob a thank-you letter, knowing the old Porsche mechanic didn’t use computers or email and wouldn’t want a phone call.


The couple will spend the winter in Florida, where Marty will take delivery of a recently purchased, super-low-mile Porsche 718 Boxster RS Spyder, the pinnacle model powered by the 911 GT3’s naturally aspirated flat-six. One of his first stops will be the Sarasota Café Racers, a “non-club club” of hardcore car enthusiasts who meet for lunch and good-natured bench racing.


Come spring, Marty and Paula will be back in their Western home and driving more tours with the red 911 Turbo and other cars.


***


Car: 1986 Porsche 911 Turbo


Name: Marty Quadland


Home: Sarasota, Florida / Heber City, Utah


Delivery Date: Fall 1986


Miles on car: About 120,000
